title: An island (24–28)
hookLine: by effort and restraint the wise make an island no flood can overwhelm

cards: In the Ganges plain, the monsoon floods can spread for miles. Fields vanish. Roads vanish.
From above, the land is a sheet of brown water.
But here and there are small patches of raised ground, where a village has built up the earth, year after year, basket by basket, so that when the water rises, there's still somewhere dry to stand.
Nobody builds that in one season. And nobody builds it during the flood.

teach.b: Verse twenty-five, in Müller's English: “By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
Four tools: rousing yourself, heedfulness, restraint and self-control. One result: an island.

teach.h: THE FLOOD: WHAT SWEEPS US ALONG.
teach.b: In the Buddha's teaching, the flood is a standing image for the currents that sweep people along: craving, views, ignorance, the endless round. You can't stop the river. You can raise the ground you stand on.

The word for island is dipa, and here's a lovely puzzle: in Pali, dipa can also mean lamp. When the Buddha, near the end of his life, told his followers to be a dipa for themselves, translators split.
Rhys Davids gave lamps; many modern translators give islands. The tradition has lived with both.

teach.h: LITTLE PANTHAKA AND THE WHITE CLOTH.
teach.b: The commentary tells verse twenty-five about a monk called Little Panthaka. For four months he couldn't memorize a single verse; it slipped away as soon as he learned the next line.

His brother, also a monk, told him to give up and go home. The Buddha found him crying outside the monastery, handed him a clean white cloth, and told him to rub it while repeating a simple phrase about removing dirt.
The cloth grew grimy in his hand, and in that small change he saw how everything changes. The story says he awakened right there.
The verses around it add that fools give themselves to carelessness, while the wise guard heedfulness like their best treasure.
Panthaka didn't build his island with scholarship. He built it with one small practice, repeated.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the island verse to describe steady daily practice as a refuge, and the story of Culapanthaka and the white cloth is a favorite example of awakening through one simple, repeated practice.

o: a quiet retreat cut off from other people and the world
raised ground the wise build so no flood sweeps them away
a lonely place where you're stranded with no way home

games.q: match the pieces of the island verses.
p: the currents that sweep people along
grew grimy as he rubbed it

s: in Pali, dipa can mean both island and lamp
that's why some translators have the Buddha say 'be lamps unto yourselves' and others 'be islands.'
Little Panthaka awakened after memorizing the whole teaching
he couldn't memorize one verse; he awakened rubbing a white cloth.
the island in verse twenty-five is built by rousing yourself, heedfulness, restraint and control

games.q: you're Little Panthaka. four months, and you still can't memorize one verse. your brother tells you to go home. what happens?
o: you go home and give up.
the Buddha gives you a white cloth to rub with a simple phrase.
you memorize it that night out of spite.
games.why: the Buddha found him, gave him a clean cloth and a phrase about removing dirt. watching the cloth grow grimy, he saw how everything changes.

practice: Think of the flood in your own life: the busiest week, the hard news, the tired evening when everything slides.
Ask what small thing, done every day, would give you somewhere dry to stand: maybe this sit, three breaths before opening email, a walk after dinner.
Choose one small enough to keep even on a bad day, and picture doing it tomorrow, and the next day, one basket of earth at a time.

wordCard.voice: An island. The raised ground the wise build, by effort and restraint, so that no flood can overwhelm them.

orig.note: Pali: island, and also lamp: the word behind 'make an island.'

carryVoice: Your line: make an island. Somewhere dry to stand, whatever the weather. Day one hundred sixty-three, done.

sources.q: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
